lead: A multilevel inverter makes AC not by jumping between two rails but by stacking many small DC steps. If the DC bus is Vdc and the output has m levels, each step is Vdc/(m−1). The waveform then looks closer to a sine, the harmonic content and dv/dt fall, and each device blocks only a fraction of the bus. Electric drives, solar farms, UPS units and HVDC links use this idea. The three common families, their level counts, and their costs in devices, capacitors and DC supplies are below.
prereq: You need: the six-step bridge in Chapter 4.2 and carrier PWM in Chapter 4.4.

sections.h3: Why many levels: small steps, small device voltages

blocks.text: A two-level inverter connects the load to either the positive or negative DC rail. The output moves in one large jump. A multilevel inverter adds intermediate rails or cells, so the same DC bus is divided into smaller steps. The load voltage climbs or falls one step at a time. The waveform is a staircase, not a square wave.
ΔV = Vdc/(m−1),   phase levels = m,   line-to-line levels = 2m−1
blocks.where: ΔV is the voltage step in volts; Vdc is the total DC bus in volts; m is the number of phase-voltage levels, with m ≥ 2.

blocks.text: With m = 3 and Vdc = 600 V, ΔV = 300 V. The phase voltage can be +300 V, 0 or −300 V. Each device in a clamped leg blocks only one step, Vdc/(m−1), not the whole bus. That is why a 600 V bus can use 300 V devices in a three-level leg.

Phase voltage has m levels. Line-to-line voltage is the difference between two phase voltages. If the phase steps are spaced by ΔV, the difference can take values from +(m−1)ΔV down to −(m−1)ΔV in steps of ΔV. The count is 2m−1 levels. For m = 3, the line voltage has five levels: +600 V, +300 V, 0, −300 V and −600 V. Do not use m for the line-to-line count.

sections.h3: Three families: diode-clamped, flying capacitor, cascaded

blocks.text: A diode-clamped leg (the three-level version is called neutral-point-clamped, NPC) uses one DC bus split by m−1 capacitors. Diodes clamp each switch node to a capacitor tap. Per leg it needs 2(m−1) active switches and (m−1)(m−2) clamping diodes. A three-level leg has four switches and two clamping diodes. It is common in medium-voltage drives because it uses one DC bus.

A flying-capacitor leg uses floating capacitors to clamp the switch nodes. It has no clamping diodes. The capacitor voltages must be precharged and balanced. Balance is harder when the load current is small or the modulation index is low.

A cascaded H-bridge uses s separate H-bridge cells per phase. Each cell has its own isolated DC source, such as a transformer winding, battery pack or PV string. A cell gives +Vcell, 0 or −Vcell. The series connection gives 2s+1 phase levels. The peak phase voltage is sVcell. For s = 3 cells of 100 V, the phase has 7 levels and a 300 V peak.

Level-shifted carrier PWM compares one sine reference with m−1 triangular carriers stacked across the range. The carriers can be in phase or shifted; the comparison decides which level is switched. Nearest level control simply rounds the reference to the nearest available level. It switches slowly and suits large m.

More levels reduce the step size. Lower step size means lower dv/dt, lower harmonic distortion and less stress on motor insulation. Each device blocks less voltage. The cost is more devices, gate drivers, capacitors, voltage sensors and control code. Capacitor voltage balance becomes a control problem. NPC has neutral-point drift. Flying-capacitor balancing is harder. Cascaded H-bridge needs isolated DC sources, which means a multi-winding transformer or separate packs.

Use multilevel inverters where the DC bus is high and waveform quality matters: medium-voltage motor drives, solar farms, UPS, HVDC and static compensators. For low-voltage single-phase work, a two-level bridge is usually cheaper. For grid current control, see Chapter 4.9.

examples.question: A three-level neutral-point-clamped inverter runs from a total DC bus Vdc = 600 V. (a) Find the voltage blocked by each active device. (b) List the phase-voltage levels. (c) List the line-to-line voltage levels. (d) A cascaded H-bridge uses 3 cells per phase, each cell with a 100 V isolated DC source. Find the number of phase levels and the peak phase voltage.
steps: The number of levels is m = 3. The step size is ΔV = Vdc/(m−1) = 600 V / 2 = 300 V.
Each active device blocks one step, so the device voltage is 300 V.
The phase voltage levels are +300 V, 0 and −300 V.
The line-to-line voltage has 2m−1 = 2×3−1 = 5 levels. They are +600 V, +300 V, 0, −300 V and −600 V.
For the cascaded converter, s = 3 cells per phase. The phase level count is 2s+1 = 2×3+1 = 7 levels.
The peak phase voltage is sVcell = 3×100 V = 300 V.
examples.answer: Each device blocks 300 V; the phase levels are +300 V, 0 and −300 V; the line-to-line voltage has 5 levels: +600 V, +300 V, 0, −300 V and −600 V; the cascaded converter has 7 phase levels and a 300 V peak phase voltage.

traps: Do not use m for line-to-line levels. A phase with m levels gives 2m−1 line-to-line levels.
Do not say each device blocks Vdc. In an m-level clamped leg the ideal block is Vdc/(m−1).
Cascaded H-bridge cells need isolated DC sources. They cannot share one common DC bus without extra isolation.

NPC has m−1 DC-bus capacitors for the whole inverter, shared by all legs, and (m−1)(m−2) clamping diodes per leg. For three-level, that is two DC-bus capacitors in total and two clamping diodes per leg.
More levels does not remove capacitor-balance control. NPC neutral-point drift and flying-capacitor balance are real control problems.

quiz.q: State the voltage step of an m-level inverter with total DC bus Vdc.
Why does a phase voltage with m levels produce a line-to-line voltage with 2m−1 levels?
quiz.a: Line-to-line voltage is the difference of two phase voltages. The difference runs from +(m−1) steps to −(m−1) steps in one-step increments, so the count is 2m−1.

quiz.q: A five-level diode-clamped inverter has Vdc = 800 V. Find the step size, the voltage blocked by each device, and the number of line-to-line levels.
quiz.a: Step = 800/(5−1) = 200 V. Each device blocks 200 V. Line-to-line levels = 2×5−1 = 9.

quiz.q: Why does a cascaded H-bridge need isolated DC sources while a diode-clamped inverter can use one DC bus?
quiz.a: Each H-bridge cell floats at a different potential in the series stack. Its DC source must be isolated from the others. An NPC leg uses capacitor taps on one common DC bus, so it does not need separate isolated sources.

quiz.q: How many clamping diodes per leg does an m-level diode-clamped inverter need?
quiz.a: It needs (m−1)(m−2) clamping diodes per leg.

quiz.q: A cascaded H-bridge has 4 cells per phase, each with a 50 V source. Find the number of phase levels, the peak phase voltage, and the number of line-to-line levels.
quiz.a: Phase levels = 2×4+1 = 9. Peak phase voltage = 4×50 = 200 V. Line-to-line levels = 2×9−1 = 17.

quiz.q: Give two benefits and two costs of increasing the number of levels in an inverter.
quiz.a: Benefits: smaller voltage step, lower dv/dt and lower harmonic distortion; each device blocks less voltage. Costs: more devices, gate drivers, capacitors, sensors and control code; capacitor voltage balance and, for cascaded cells, isolated DC supplies become harder.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry has moved beyond the three basic families: the modular multilevel converter (MMC) stacks many identical submodules and is used in HVDC, and the active neutral-point-clamped (ANPC) leg improves loss distribution in three-level drives. Wide-bandgap devices such as SiC MOSFETs let multilevel legs switch faster, so the line filter shrinks. Research topics include capacitor voltage balancing, model predictive control, fault-tolerant cells and reduced-device topologies. Search next for “modular multilevel converter,” “ANPC inverter” and “nearest level control.”
